source.title: Regularization Trade-offs with Fake Features
source.authors: Martin Hellkvist; Ayça Özçelikkale; A. Ahlén

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; some mathematical formatting and figure-label superscripts are garbled in the extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures generalization error while varying the number of fake features in a finite-dimensional linear ridge-regression setting. This conceptually tests double descent in a model class beyond deep networks, and tests how regularization affects the curve.
record.gate_note: The paper cites earlier double-descent results, but those cited results are not rows. Its own numerical results vary fake-feature count and ridge regularization and report generalization error.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps model capacity (fake features pF) in finite-dimensional misspecified linear ridge regression. It reports empirical generalization error showing a peak at the interpolation threshold (pF=100, n=200) and a second descent, and how the ridge parameter dampens that peak. This is a new setting with its own results on V4 and V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that fake features provide implicit regularization that can compensate for a small ridge parameter, giving the lowest error at pF>10^3 for λ/n∈{0,10}. The optimal λ depends on the number of fake features. With enough explicit regularization, more fake features may increase error, and large λ dampens the interpolation-threshold peak and lowers variance.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses synthetic finite-dimensional linear ridge regression with Gaussian features and fake features, rather than deep-network scaling or training experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The generalization-error curve changes with the ridge parameter; the paper reports that larger values dampen the peak and that the best ridge parameter depends on the number of fake features.
record.problems: The numerical evidence is reported as plots rather than exact curve values in the text. The tested setting is a specific synthetic linear-regression setup, and the extraction garbles some figure-label superscripts.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 1 reports generalization error versus ridge parameter for several fake-feature counts, and the text discusses shifting minima. It does not measure the size-wise interpolation peak named by V4 or V6, so it is not included as a row for those versions.

untested.parts: Label noise was not varied as a driver of the peak, and triple or multiple descent was not tested. No error-versus-pF curve at the optimally tuned λ is reported, so 'disappears under optimal tuning' is not directly tested.
Only isotropic Gaussian linear ridge regression with fake features was tested; no other model classes.
Not tested; n is fixed at 200.

missing.what: Standard deviation of generalization error is 'extremely large' at the threshold pF=100 with λ=0. It decreases as λ or pF increases, consistent with a variance-driven peak.

Error versus λ for pF ∈ {0,100,300,500}: the optimal λ and the minimum error both increase with pF. This is relevant to optimally tuned regularization but is not reported as an error-versus-pF curve at optimal λ.
Theorem 1 argues analytically that λ must be large enough to bound the error near the interpolation threshold, and that fake features regularize the bound.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3: the study is a new misspecified-linear setting, not the originals' method. The λ/n=10 label in r2 is confirmed by the text. Evidence is figure-only, with M=100 realizations and n=200.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses linear ridge regression, not deep networks.
No training-epoch or training-time sweep is reported.
The number of training samples is not varied to test whether more data raises test error.
The study tests a linear ridge-regression setting with Gaussian features, not other model classes generally.
The study does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.

The study varies ridge regularization and reports its effect on the error curve. It does not vary label noise to establish the cause of the peak, test multiple descent, or test whether optimally tuned regularization eliminates the peak.
The study does not measure complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether that recasting makes the curve U-shaped.

relationships.condition: Linear ridge regression with fake features, small regularization (λ/n ∈ {0, 10})
relationships.reason: Error peaks at the interpolation threshold pF=100 and falls again, with the lowest error at pF>10^3 (r1, r2; Fig. 2, text).
relationships.display_finding: Error peaked at pF=100 and declined again, reaching its lowest value at pF>10³.

relationships.reason: The peak is dampened, and the authors state the smallest pF gives the lowest error, so the benefit of capacity past interpolation depends on λ (r3, r4).
relationships.display_finding: The peak weakened, and the smallest pF achieved the lowest error.

relationships.condition: Regularization dependence of the peak, across tested λ values
relationships.reason: The peak is seen at λ/n∈{0,10} and dampened at λ/n∈{10^2,10^3}. Removal under optimal tuning is not shown (r1–r4).
relationships.display_finding: Peaks appeared at λ/n∈{0,10} and weakened at λ/n∈{10²,10³}, without demonstrated removal through optimal tuning.
